mainTopic: רבי יהושע's four cases of פטור מדיני אדם וחייב בדיני שמים, and רבה on a breached sheep pen
overview: The amud continues a ברייתא in which רבי יהושע lists four acts that are exempt in a human court but liable before Heaven. These are breaking a fence in front of an animal, bending someone's grain toward a fire, hiring false witnesses, and knowing testimony but not testifying. For each act, the גמרא narrows the case so that a human court could not make the person pay: a shaky wall, an unusual wind (or, for רב אשי, a hidden item), witnesses hired for someone else, and a single witness. The גמרא then points to five more cases with the same ruling and asks why the list stops at four. It answers that the list is selective. These four were taught because each comes with an excuse that might seem to free the person even before Heaven, and the גמרא shows the excuse for each one. Next the גמרא returns to the משנה about a sheep pen whose wall was breached. רבה's comment about an animal that dug its way out raises the question of negligence followed by accident. So the גמרא moves רבה's words to the later case of an animal left in the sun: the owner is liable even if it dug, because a suffering animal will try any way out. Finally the גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: if bandits took the animal out, the bandits are liable.

steps.title: Breaking a fence: the case is an unstable wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its answer about one who breaks down a fence in front of another's animal: the case is a wall that was already shaky.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about an unstable wall.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes an answer that started just before. It explains why someone who breaks a fence is exempt in בית דין: the wall was falling apart anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wall had been strong, breaking it would be real damage, and he would have to pay in a human court. Because the wall was shaky, he did not really destroy anything of value. That is why only Heaven holds him responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: An unstable, shaky wall that would fall soon anyway
Exempt from paying in a human court

phrases.english: With an unstable wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer to the question about the fence case, which was asked just before this section
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The fence case is about a wall that was already unstable, so no real damage was done

steps.title: What is the case of bending grain before a fire?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the ברייתא means by bending someone's grain toward a fire. It rejects the case of a normal wind, because then he would be liable in a human court too.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'One who bends his friend's standing grain toward a fire.' What is the case? If you say the fire would reach it with a normal wind, then he should be liable in a human court too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next case in the ברייתא and asks what situation it means. It tests one possible case and pushes it away, which sets up the real answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose a normal, expected wind would carry the fire to the bent grain. Then bending it is a clear, direct cause of the damage, and a human court would make him pay. That does not fit a ברייתא that says he is exempt in a human court, so this case must be wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master said': the formula for quoting a line from a ברייתא already mentioned
What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?
If you say: introduces a suggested case that will be tested

phrases.english: The Master said:
One who bends his friend's standing grain
toward the fire.
What is the case?
If you say that the fire would reach it with a normal wind,
then he should be liable in a human court too!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: הַכּוֹפֵף קָמָתוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ בִּפְנֵי הַדְּלֵיקָה. הֵיכִי דָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next case in the same ברייתא
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What situation of bending grain toward a fire leaves him exempt in a human court?

steps.title: The fire would reach it only with an unusual wind
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is where only an unusual wind would bring the fire to the grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is where the fire would reach it only with an unusual wind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the right case: the fire could reach the grain only if a rare, unexpected wind came.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an unusual wind, the damage is too far removed for a human court to make him pay. He still put the grain in a risky spot, and it did burn. So Heaven holds him responsible, just as the ברייתא says.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather: brings in the correct answer after a rejected one

phrases.english: Rather, it is where the fire would reach it only with an unusual wind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 2 after its first suggested case was rejected
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא means a case where only an unusual wind would bring the fire to the grain

steps.title: רב אשי: the case is about a hidden item
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains the case another way. The ברייתא is about a hidden item: by bending the grain over someone's item, he made it a 'hidden item' in the fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אשי said: it was said about a hidden item, because he made it into something hidden in the fire.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different explanation of the same line in the ברייתא. In his reading, the bending covered someone's item, so that item became a 'hidden item' in the fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule that the one who set the fire does not pay for items hidden inside the grain. By bending the grain over the item, this person turned it into a hidden item, so the owner loses his right to be paid. The person did not burn it himself, so a human court cannot charge him, but he is responsible before Heaven.

keyTerms.meaning: A hidden item (covered inside the grain)
It was said / it was taught

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not saying the grain itself was bent toward the fire. He is saying the bending covered someone's item and made it 'hidden', which is a different kind of loss.

phrases.english: And Rav Ashi said:
It was said about a hidden item,
because he made it into a hidden item in the fire.
phrases.notes: By bending the grain over the item, he covered it. Now it counts as hidden, and the one who set the fire doesn't pay for hidden things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different way to explain the case asked about in step 2, instead of the unusual-wind answer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case is about bending the grain toward the fire, with an unusual wind
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is where bending the grain made someone's item 'hidden', so its owner cannot collect from the one who set the fire

steps.title: What is the case of hiring false witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא means by hiring false witnesses. It rejects hiring them for himself, because then he must give back the money and is liable in a human court.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'One who hires false witnesses.' What is the case? If you say he hired them for himself, he has to pay back the money, so he should be liable in a human court too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next case in the ברייתא and asks what situation it means. It rejects the obvious case, which sets up the real answer next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he hired the witnesses to win money for himself, he is holding money that is not his. A human court would make him give it back. That cannot be the case of a ברייתא that says he is exempt in a human court.

keyTerms.meaning: He has to pay back money

phrases.english: The Master said:
One who hires false witnesses.
What is the case?
If you say he hired them for himself,
he has to pay back the money,
so he should be liable in a human court too!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: הַשּׂוֹכֵר עֵדֵי שֶׁקֶר. הֵיכִי דָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next case in the same ברייתא, using the same question pattern as step 2
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What situation of hiring false witnesses leaves him exempt in a human court?

steps.title: He hired the witnesses for someone else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he hired the false witnesses to help another person.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he hired them for his friend.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the right case: the person hired false witnesses so that someone else would win.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the one who hired the witnesses gained no money, so a human court has nothing to take back from him. Still, he caused a real loss through lies, so Heaven holds him responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: For his friend (for someone else's benefit)

steps.whatToRemember: Each case in this ברייתא is narrowed so that the damage is too indirect for a human court: a wall that was already shaky, an unusual wind (or, for רב אשי, a hidden item), and false witnesses hired for someone else. In every case, Heaven still holds the person responsible.

phrases.english: Rather, he hired them for his friend.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 5 after its first suggested case was rejected
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא means a case where he hired false witnesses for someone else's benefit

steps.title: Which witness does the ברייתא mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the ברייתא means by 'one who knows testimony and does not testify.' It rejects the case of two witnesses, because that is already a clear Torah sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא says that one who knows testimony for his fellow and does not testify for him is exempt in a human court but liable in Heaven. What case is this? If it means two witnesses, that is obvious. It is a Torah law: 'If he does not tell, he shall bear his sin.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the ברייתא's next case, the witness who stays silent. It asks what situation is meant and rules out the case of two witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two witnesses together can make the other side pay. If they stay quiet, the פסוק in ויקרא already says they sin. So the ברייתא would gain nothing by teaching that case, and it must mean something less obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing?
If you say, if we suggest
It is obvious, so why teach it?
From the Torah, a Torah law

phrases.english: And one who knows testimony for his fellow
and does not testify for him.
With what case are we dealing?
If we say it is about two witnesses, it is obvious!
It is a Torah law:
"If he does not tell, he shall bear his sin"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as steps 2 and 5: the גמרא takes the next case in the ברייתא and asks what situation it means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of witness is meant in the case of one who stays silent?

steps.title: It means a single witness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a single witness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is talking about one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: the case is a single witness who does not come forward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One witness alone cannot make someone pay, so the Torah sin in the פסוק does not apply to him. Still, his testimony could have forced the other side to swear or pay. By staying quiet he caused a loss in an indirect way, so he is חייב בדיני שמים.

keyTerms.meaning: A single witness, whose testimony can require the other side to take an oath

steps.whatToRemember: A silent pair of witnesses breaks a Torah law. A silent single witness is the ברייתא's case: exempt in a human court, but liable in Heaven for the loss he caused.

phrases.english: Rather, it is about one witness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case is a single witness. The Torah sin does not apply to him, but he still caused a loss indirectly.

steps.title: Why doesn't the list include working with מי חטאת?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the ברייתא's list is complete. It gives a memory aid and points to a missing case: one who does work with מי חטאת or a פרת חטאת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there nothing more? But there is more! (Memory aid: one who does, with poison, and an agent, his fellow, is broken.) One who does work with purification water or with the red heifer is exempt in a human court but liable in Heaven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's list. Other cases fit the same rule, so why weren't they listed? This step begins a list of such cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא seemed to give a full list of 'exempt in a human court, liable in Heaven' cases. The גמרא brings a case that fits but is missing: using מי חטאת or a פרת חטאת for work, which makes it unfit and causes a loss. The memory aid tells us five extra cases are coming.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid listing the coming cases by key words
Purification water mixed with the red heifer's ashes

keyTerms.term: פָּטוּר מִדִּינֵי אָדָם וְחַיָּיב בְּדִינֵי שָׁמַיִם
keyTerms.meaning: Exempt in a human court but liable in Heaven

steps.confusionAlert: The memory aid is not a ruling. It is only a list of key words that points to the five cases the גמרא is about to bring.

phrases.english: And is there nothing more?
But there is
(Memory aid: one who does, with poison,
phrases.notes: This is a memory aid, one key word for each case coming up. Some versions have these words in round brackets and some don't.

phrases.english: and an agent, his fellow, is broken.)
one who does work with the purification water
or with the red heifer of purification:
phrases.notes: Doing work with them makes them unfit to use, so the owner loses them.

phrases.english: he is exempt in a human court,
but liable in Heaven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After all the ברייתא's cases have been explained, the גמרא asks why its list is not longer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The completeness of the ברייתא's list of cases.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Working with מי חטאת or a פרת חטאת fits the same rule, yet the ברייתא leaves it out.

steps.title: Another missing case: poison in front of an animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a second missing case: one who puts deadly poison in front of his fellow's animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is also one who puts deadly poison in front of his fellow's animal. He is exempt in a human court but liable in Heaven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the same challenge and adds the second case from the memory aid, the poison case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The animal ate the poison on its own, so a human court does not hold the man liable. He still set up the animal's death, so Heaven holds him responsible. This is one more case the ברייתא could have listed but didn't.

phrases.english: But there is one who puts deadly poison
in front of his fellow's animal:
he is exempt in a human court,
but liable in Heaven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second example to the challenge begun in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The completeness of the ברייתא's list of cases.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Placing poison in front of another's animal also fits the rule but is missing from the ברייתא.

steps.title: Missing case: sending fire with a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a third case missing from the list: one who sends fire through a חרש שוטה וקטן. He is exempt in human court but liable in Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is also the case of one who sends a fire in the hand of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor. He is exempt by human courts and liable by the laws of Heaven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps attacking the list of four in the ברייתא. Here is another case that fits the same pattern but is not on the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חרש שוטה וקטן is not legally responsible, and the sender did not light the damage himself, so a human court cannot make him pay. Still, he caused the fire, so he is liable in Heaven. That fits רבי יהושע's category, so why is it missing?

keyTerms.meaning: But there is also… (brings a missing case)
A deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, who are not legally responsible
Liable by the laws of Heaven

phrases.english: But there is one who sends the fire
in the hand of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor
he is exempt by human courts
and liable by the laws of Heaven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third missing case after the ones in steps 9 and 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in the ברייתא that there are only four such cases.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Here is another case with the same ruling, so the list of four seems incomplete.

steps.title: Missing case: one who frightens his fellow
steps.stepSummary: A fourth missing case: one who frightens his friend is exempt in human court but liable in Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is also the case of one who frightens his fellow. He is exempt by human courts and liable by the laws of Heaven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings yet another case that matches the pattern but is not on רבי יהושע's list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Scaring someone can cause him harm, but a human court does not make the scarer pay. Since he is still liable in Heaven, this case also fits the category.

phrases.english: But there is one who frightens his fellow
he is exempt by human courts
and liable by the laws of Heaven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another missing case in the same series of challenges.
steps.kashyaTarget: The completeness of the list of four in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Frightening someone has the same two-part ruling, yet it is not listed.

steps.title: Missing case: a broken jug or a fallen camel left in the public street
steps.stepSummary: A fifth missing case: someone whose jug broke or whose camel fell in רשות הרבים and he left it there. רבי מאיר makes him pay; חכמים say he is exempt in human court but liable in Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is also the case of one whose jug broke in the public domain and he did not remove it, or whose camel fell and he did not stand it up. רבי מאיר holds him liable for the damage it causes, and חכמים say: he is exempt by human courts and liable by the laws of Heaven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a final missing case. According to חכמים, it also fits the pattern 'exempt in human court, liable in Heaven.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The jug broke or the camel fell by accident, but the owner then left it in the way and someone got hurt. רבי מאיר says he pays. חכמים say a human court cannot make him pay, but Heaven holds him responsible. So according to חכמים, this case belongs on the list too.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, a public street

phrases.english: But there is one whose jug broke
in the public domain, and he did not remove it
or his camel fell and he did not stand it up
Rabbi Meir holds him liable for the damage they cause
phrases.notes: "They" means the broken pieces of the jug or the fallen camel, when someone trips over them.

phrases.english: and the Rabbis say:
he is exempt by human courts
and liable by the laws of Heaven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The last missing case in the series. After this, the גמרא answers all the challenges together.
steps.kashyaTarget: The completeness of the list of four in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to חכמים, this case has exactly the same ruling, so it should have been listed.

steps.title: Yes, there are many cases, but these four needed to be taught
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא admits there are many more such cases. רבי יהושע chose these four because without them we might think there is no liability in Heaven at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, in any event there are many. But these he needed to state. You might have said that he should not be liable even by the laws of Heaven, so he teaches us that he is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers all the missing-case challenges at once. The list was never meant to be complete.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is not counting every case. It picks the four where someone might think the person is completely free, even in Heaven. In the other cases, liability in Heaven is obvious, so there was no need to teach them.

keyTerms.meaning: In any event, at any rate

steps.whatToRemember: The list of four in the ברייתא is a selective list, not a complete count. These four cases are the ones where you might have thought there is no liability even in Heaven.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the גמרא is rejecting the other cases. It agrees they are also 'exempt in human court, liable in Heaven.' They just did not need to be said.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a common way the גמרא handles a list that seems to leave things out: the list only includes cases with a special lesson.

phrases.english: Yes, in any event there are many
but these he needed to state
phrases.notes: "These" are the four cases רבי יהושע listed in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: for you might have said
that even by the laws of Heaven he should not be liable
so he teaches us that he is.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers all the missing-case challenges from steps 9 to 13 together.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Admits the facts but changes the purpose of the list: it is selective, not complete.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's 'four' was meant as a complete count of all such cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: The four cases were chosen because one might think there is no liability even in Heaven. Other cases exist but did not need to be taught.

steps.title: Why the case of breaking a fence was needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why רבי יהושע needed to teach the case of one who breaks a fence in front of his friend's animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who breaks down a fence in front of his friend's animal: you might have thought that since the fence was ready to fall anyway, he did nothing, so he should not be liable even in דיני שמים. That is why רבי יהושע teaches that he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts going through רבי יהושע's four cases one by one. For the fence case, it shows why we might have thought he is not liable at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fence was already shaky and about to collapse, so the person could argue he barely changed anything. Because of that argument, we might have thought he is free even in דיני שמים. רבי יהושע teaches that he is still liable in דיני שמים.

keyTerms.meaning: One who breaks down a fence
You might have said / you might have thought
It is standing ready to be torn down (about to fall anyway)
The laws of Heaven, liability before ה׳ even when a human court cannot make you pay
It teaches us (that the 'you might have thought' idea is wrong)

phrases.english: One who breaks down a fence in front of his fellow's animal:
You might have said:
Since it is standing ready to be torn down,
What did he really do?
So he should not be liable even in the laws of Heaven;
It teaches us that he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills in the general answer of step 14 for the first case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining a חידוש: showing what mistake the case prevents
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the fence was about to fall anyway, he did nothing and is not even liable in דיני שמים.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is liable in דיני שמים.

steps.title: Why the case of bending a friend's grain was needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why רבי יהושע needed to teach the case of one who bends his friend's standing grain toward a fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who bends his friend's standing grain: you might have thought he can say, 'How was I supposed to know an unusual wind would come?' So he should not be liable even in דיני שמים. That is why רבי יהושע teaches that he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second case and gives the excuse that might have freed the person completely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bending the grain only caused damage because an unusual wind carried the fire to it. The person could claim he could not have predicted such a wind. רבי יהושע teaches that this excuse does not free him in דיני שמים.

keyTerms.meaning: An unusual wind, one that does not normally blow

phrases.english: Also, one who bends his fellow's standing grain:
You might have said: let him say,
"Did I know
that an unusual wind would come?"
And so he should not be liable even in the laws of Heaven;
It teaches us that he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as step 15, applied to the second case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining a חידוש: showing what mistake the case prevents
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He can say he could not foresee an unusual wind, so he is not even liable in דיני שמים.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is liable in דיני שמים.

steps.title: The covered item case according to רב אשי
steps.stepSummary: According to רב אשי, who explained the case as being about a hidden item, the גמרא explains what mistake רבי יהושע's teaching prevents.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רב אשי, who said the case was also stated about a hidden item: you might have thought the person could say, 'I covered it up for you,' so he should not be liable even in דיני שמים. That is why רבי יהושע teaches that he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different 'you might have thought' reason for the grain case, following רב אשי's way of explaining it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב אשי's reading, the person covered his friend's item so it was hidden when the fire came. He could argue that he covered it to help, to protect it. רבי יהושע teaches that he is still liable in דיני שמים.

keyTerms.meaning: I covered it up for you

phrases.english: And according to רב אשי, who said
that it was also stated about a hidden item,
You might have said that he can claim:
"I covered it up for you,"
And so he should not be liable even in the laws of Heaven;
It teaches us that he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַב אָשֵׁי – דְּאָמַר נָמֵי טָמוּן אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternate 'you might have thought' for the grain case, following רב אשי's reading.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining a חידוש according to an alternate reading of the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He can claim he covered the item to protect it, so he is not even liable in דיני שמים.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is liable in דיני שמים.

steps.title: Why the case of hiring false witnesses was needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why רבי יהושע needed to teach the case of one who hires false witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: And also one who hires false witnesses: you might have thought he can say, 'When the words of the teacher and the words of the student conflict, whose words do we listen to?' The witnesses should have listened to ה׳, so it is their fault, and he should not be liable even in דיני שמים. That is why רבי יהושע teaches that he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third of רבי יהושע's four cases, hiring false witnesses. The fourth case, the silent witness, comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hirer could blame the witnesses: ה׳, the 'teacher,' told them not to lie, and they chose to listen to him, the 'student,' instead. So we might have thought all the blame is on them. רבי יהושע teaches that the hirer is still liable in דיני שמים.

keyTerms.meaning: The words of the teacher and the words of the student
Whose words do we listen to?

phrases.english: And also one who hires false witnesses:
You might have said: let him say,
"The words of the teacher and the words of the student,
phrases.notes: The teacher is ה׳, who forbade lying. The student is the man who hired the witnesses.

phrases.english: whose words do we listen to?"
And so he should not be liable even in the laws of Heaven;
It teaches us that he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַשּׂוֹכֵר עֵדֵי שֶׁקֶר נָמֵי – מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא, לֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series begun in step 15 with the third of רבי יהושע's four cases; step 19 gives the fourth.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining a חידוש: showing what mistake the case prevents
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The witnesses should have listened to ה׳, so the blame is only theirs, and the hirer is not even liable in דיני שמים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The hirer is liable in דיני שמים.

steps.title: Why teach the case of a witness who does not testify
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע had to teach that a silent witness is liable in Heaven. Otherwise we might think he could excuse himself, since the other side might have sworn falsely anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one who knows testimony for his friend and does not testify also needed to be taught. You might have thought the witness could say: 'Who says that if I had come and testified, the other side would have admitted? Maybe he would have sworn a false oath.' So you might think he is not liable even in Heaven. רבי יהושע teaches us that he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the fourth and final case. The גמרא shows what mistake רבי יהושע's teaching prevents for a witness who stays silent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witness's excuse is that his testimony might not have helped, because the other side could have sworn falsely and walked away. רבי יהושע rejects that excuse. Since his silence still caused a possible loss, he is liable בדיני שמים.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces the mistaken idea)

steps.whatToRemember: All four of רבי יהושע's cases share the same reason: each one has an excuse that might make us think there is no liability at all, even in Heaven. רבי יהושע teaches that the person is still liable בדיני שמים.

phrases.english: And one who knows testimony for his friend
and does not testify for him, also —
you might have said:
"Who says that if I had come
and testified for him, he would have admitted?
phrases.notes: The one who 'would have admitted' is the other side in the case, the person the testimony was against.

phrases.english: Perhaps he would have sworn falsely,"
and so even in the laws of Heaven he should not be liable;
so he teaches us that he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיּוֹדֵעַ עֵדוּת לַחֲבֵירוֹ וְאֵינוֹ מֵעִיד לוֹ, נָמֵי – מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the pattern of steps 15-18, now explaining the fourth case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the case is needed to block a mistaken assumption (מהו דתימא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The witness is fully exempt, because his testimony might not have helped.

steps.title: רבה explains the משנה: the animal dug under the wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a pen that was breached at night or by bandits. רבה says the first case means the animal dug under the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: if the pen was breached at night, or bandits breached it, and so on, the owner is exempt. רבה said: this is only when the animal dug under the wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and quotes רבה's explanation of the first case. רבה limits it to a pen whose wall fell because the animal dug under it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה exempts the owner when the pen broke at night. רבה adds a condition: the animal tunneled under the wall and brought it down. This sets up the next question about what happens when the animal did not tunnel.

keyTerms.meaning: Was breached (the pen's wall broke open)
An אמורא who gives this explanation

phrases.english: If it was breached at night
phrases.notes: 'It' is the wall of the sheep pen in the משנה.

phrases.english: or bandits breached it, etc.
Rabba said:
And this is when it tunneled.
phrases.notes: The animal dug under the wall, and that is what made it fall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the גמרא returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's exemption for a pen breached at night applies when the animal tunneled under the wall.

steps.title: If the animal did not dig, why would he be liable with a strong wall?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבה means the owner is liable when the animal did not dig. With a strong wall, that makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if the animal did not dig, what then? Is the owner liable? What is the case? If you say it was a strong wall, then even if the animal did not dig, why should he be liable? What more could he have done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה's limit. It begins testing which kind of wall רבה could be talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's words suggest that if the animal did not dig, the owner is liable. With a strong, healthy wall, though, the owner did everything right and should be exempt no matter what. So רבה cannot be talking about a strong wall.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? (how exactly does it look)
What should he have done? (he did all he could)

phrases.english: But if it did not tunnel, what — is he liable?!
What is the case?
If you say it was a strong wall —
then when it did not tunnel, why is he liable?
What should he have done?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges what follows from רבה's condition in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The implication of רבה's statement, that the owner is liable if the animal did not tunnel.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With a strong wall the owner did nothing wrong, so he should be exempt even without tunneling.

steps.title: With a weak wall, why is he exempt even if the animal dug?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries a weak wall instead. Then the owner was careless from the start, so why should digging exempt him?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it was a weak wall. But then, even when the animal dug, why is he exempt? This is a case that began with negligence and ended with an accident!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the other option, a weak wall, and finds a problem with it too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving a weak wall is careless (פשיעה), even though the animal digging is an accident (אונס). That makes this a case of תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס, and such a case might bring liability. So רבה's exemption for a dug-under weak wall is hard to explain.

keyTerms.meaning: It began with negligence and ended with an accident

steps.confusionAlert: The damage did not happen because the wall was weak. It happened because the animal dug, which is an accident. The question is whether the owner's earlier carelessness still makes him responsible.

phrases.english: Rather, it was a weak wall —
then when it tunneled, why is he exempt?
It began with negligence and ended with an accident!
phrases.notes: The negligence is leaving a weak wall. The accident is the animal digging underneath.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בְּכוֹתֶל רָעוּעַ – כִּי חָתְרָה אַמַּאי פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the second option after step 21 ruled out a strong wall.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's exemption when the animal tunneled under a weak wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner was careless to begin with, so the case is תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס, which may bring liability.

steps.title: The challenge is strongest for the view that holds the owner liable
steps.stepSummary: רבה works for the view that exempts a case of negligence followed by accident. For the view that holds such a case liable, there is a problem, which step 24 answers.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for the one who says a case that began with negligence and ended with an accident is exempt. But for the one who says such a case is liable, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sharpens its question. It shows exactly which opinion has trouble with רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known dispute about תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס. For the view that exempts it, רבה's ruling fits. For the view that holds it liable, רבה's exemption seems wrong, and the גמרא now needs an answer for that view.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well for the one who says
What is there to say? (there is still a problem)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רבה's explanation of the משנה depends on how one rules in the wider dispute about תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס.

phrases.english: This works well for the one who says:
if it began with negligence and ended with an accident, he is exempt;
but according to the one who says:
if it began with negligence and ended with an accident, he is liable —
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the challenge from step 22 to one side of the dispute.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's exemption, according to the view that holds תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By that view, the owner's first negligence makes him liable even though the final cause was an accident, so the exemption should not hold.

steps.title: רבה's statement belongs to the later case of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The first case of the משנה is about a strong wall, and the owner is exempt even without digging. רבה's "even if it dug" was said about the later case, where the animal was left in the sun.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, our משנה is about a strong wall, and the owner is exempt even if the animal did not dig. רבה's statement was said about the later part of the משנה: if he left it in the sun, or handed it to a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, and it went out and caused damage, he is liable. רבה said: even if it dug.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the earlier questions by moving רבה's statement to a different part of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, רבה seemed to say the first case is only exempt when the animal dug, and that caused the problems in steps 21-23. Now the first case simply exempts the owner with a strong wall, dug or not. רבה's "even if it dug" now makes the later case stricter: an owner who left his animal in the sun is liable even if it dug its way out.

keyTerms.meaning: It (the animal) dug or tunneled under the wall
The later part of a משנה
A deaf-mute, an insane person, and a minor (people not legally responsible)

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the wording change. In the first version, רבה said "וְהוּא שֶׁחָתְרָה" (only when it dug), about the exempt first case. In the new version, he said "וַאֲפִילּוּ חָתְרָה" (even if it dug), about the later case where the owner is liable.

phrases.english: Rather, our משנה is about a strong wall,
and [the owner is exempt] even if it did not dig.
phrases.notes: The words "the owner is exempt" are left out, but the גמרא means them here.

phrases.english: And when Rabba's statement was said,
it was said about the later part:
If he left it in the sun,
or handed it over to a deaf-mute, an insane person, or a minor,
and it went out and caused damage, he is liable.
Rabba said: and even if it dug.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the unresolved question of step 23 by giving up the old placement of רבה's statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moving a statement to a different clause of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבה was explaining the first case, saying the owner is exempt only if the animal dug.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first case exempts with a strong wall even without digging. רבה was really making the later case stricter: liable even if it dug.

steps.title: Why רבה needed to say "even if it dug"
steps.stepSummary: Without digging, liability is obvious because it is all negligence. The new point is that even with digging, it is not counted as negligence followed by accident. It is all negligence.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not needed to say the owner is liable where the animal did not dig, since the whole thing is negligence. The point is that even if it dug, he is also liable. You might have said this is a case that starts with negligence and ends with an accident. So רבה teaches us that it is all negligence.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what new point רבה is teaching with the words "even if it dug."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Digging could look like an accident that came after the owner's carelessness. That kind of case is the disputed case of תחילתו בפשיעה וסופו באונס from step 23. רבה avoids that dispute by saying the digging is itself part of the negligence, so everyone agrees the owner is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not needed to say (this is obvious)
Starting with negligence and ending with an accident

steps.whyThisMatters: By calling the whole event פשיעה, רבה's ruling does not depend on the dispute about negligence followed by accident that troubled the גמרא in step 23.

phrases.english: It is not needed to say where it did not dig,
since the whole thing is negligence,
but even if it dug, [he is liable] too.
You might have said:
it is a case that started with negligence
and ended with an accident;

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּכוּלַּהּ פְּשִׁיעָה הִיא,
phrases.english: it teaches us that it is all negligence.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the new point in רבה's statement, now that it has been moved to the later case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An owner who left his animal in the sun is liable even if it dug out. The whole event counts as negligence, not negligence followed by accident.

steps.title: Asking why digging still counts as negligence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason that the digging is counted as part of the owner's negligence.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next step by asking why the whole event counts as negligence, even with the digging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 25 stated the rule but did not explain it. This short question asks for the logic that turns an unusual act, digging, into part of the owner's carelessness.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the ruling in step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is digging out not counted as an accident that came after the negligence?

steps.title: The owner should have known a suffering animal would escape any way it could
steps.stepSummary: The one who suffered the damage can tell the owner: you knew that once you left it in the sun, it would use every trick to get out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the one who suffered the damage can say to the owner: You surely knew that once you left it in the sun, it would use every trick it could and get out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason: an animal suffering in the sun will try anything to escape, so even digging was predictable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An accident is something the owner could not expect. Here the owner caused the animal's distress, so any way of escaping, even digging, was something he should have expected. That makes the whole event his negligence.

keyTerms.meaning: A trick or means; any way possible

steps.whatToRemember: The first case: strong wall, owner exempt even without digging. The later case: animal left in the sun, owner liable even if it dug. The suffering he caused makes any escape predictable, so it is all פשיעה.

phrases.english: Because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: "He" is the one whose property was damaged, speaking to the animal's owner.

phrases.english: You surely knew
that once you left it in the sun,
every trick that it could possibly do
it would do, and get out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Leaving the animal in the sun makes any escape, even digging, foreseeable. So the whole event is the owner's negligence.

steps.title: Next line of the משנה: bandits who took the animal out
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: if bandits took the sheep out, the bandits are liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If bandits took it out, the bandits are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on and quotes the next line of the משנה, setting up a new discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was the owner's liability when the animal got out by itself. Here people took it out. Since they took control of it, the liability moves from the owner to them.

phrases.english: If bandits took it out, the bandits are liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the discussion of רבה and goes back to quoting the משנה for a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When bandits take the animal out of the pen, they, not the owner, are liable for the damage it causes.
